Water Resources

Three-fourths of the earth’s surface is water, yet regions run dry. This chapter explains water scarcity, the argument for and against large multi-purpose projects, and the extraordinary tradition of rainwater harvesting that India is now reviving.

Chapter Overview

What this chapter is about, at a glance

You already know that three-fourths of the earth’s surface is covered with water, but only a small proportion of it accounts for freshwater that can be put to use. This freshwater is mainly obtained from surface run-off and groundwater, which are continually renewed and recharged through the hydrological cycle. All water moves within the hydrological cycle, ensuring that water is a renewable resource.

If water is renewable and so abundant, why do countries and regions suffer from water scarcity? The chapter answers this in two parts: quantitative scarcity (over-exploitation, excessive use, unequal access, growing population) and qualitative scarcity (water made unusable by pollution).

It then examines how we conserve and manage water: the tradition of hydraulic structures from the first century B.C. onwards, modern dams and multi-purpose river projects (Bhakra–Nangal, Hirakud, Sardar Sarovar), the criticism of large dams, and government programmes such as the Jal Jeevan Mission, Atal Bhujal Yojana and Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana.

The last part is rainwater harvesting: guls and kuls, inundation channels, khadins and johads, the underground tankas of Rajasthan, rooftop harvesting in Shillong and Gendathur, Tamil Nadu’s law, and the 200-year-old bamboo drip irrigation of Meghalaya.

Freshwater sources

Surface run-off and groundwater, renewed and recharged through the hydrological cycle.

Water scarcity

Caused by over-exploitation, excessive use and unequal access — and also by bad quality of water.

Irrigated agriculture

The largest consumer of water.

Dam

A barrier across flowing water that obstructs, directs or retards the flow, often creating a reservoir, lake or impoundment.

Nehru’s phrase

Dams are the “temples of modern India”.

Jal Jeevan Mission

Every rural household to get potable piped water at 55 litres per capita per day.

Tamil Nadu

First state to make rooftop rainwater harvesting compulsory for all houses.

Gendathur, Karnataka

About 200 households harvest rainwater; the village is described as “rich in rainwater”.

Water as a Renewable Resource

Three-fourths of the earth’s surface is covered with water, but only a small proportion of it accounts for freshwater that can be put to use. This freshwater is mainly obtained from surface run-off and groundwater that is continually being renewed and recharged through the hydrological cycle. All water moves within the hydrological cycle, ensuring that water is a renewable resource.

It is predicted that by 2025, nearly two billion people will live in absolute water scarcity.

Water Scarcity and the Need for Water Conservation and Management

Given the abundance and renewability of water, it is difficult to imagine that we may suffer from water scarcity. The moment we speak of water shortages, we immediately associate it with regions having low rainfall or those that are drought prone. We instantaneously visualise the deserts of Rajasthan and women balancing many “matkas” (earthen pots) used for collecting and storing water and travelling long distances to get water. True, the availability of water resources varies over space and time, mainly due to variations in seasonal and annual precipitation — but water scarcity in most cases is caused by over-exploitation, excessive use and unequal access to water among different social groups.

Where is water scarcity likely to occur? Freshwater can be obtained directly from precipitation, surface run-off and groundwater. Many of our cities have ample water resources but still face water scarcity. Water scarcity may be an outcome of a large and growing population and consequent greater demands for water, and unequal access to it. A large population requires more water not only for domestic use but also to produce more food. Hence, to facilitate higher food-grain production, water resources are being over-exploited to expand irrigated areas for dry-season agriculture. Irrigated agriculture is the largest consumer of water.

It is now necessary to revolutionise agriculture through developing drought-resistant crops and dry farming techniques. You may have seen in many television advertisements that most farmers have their own wells and tube-wells in their farms for irrigation to increase their produce — but this may lead to falling groundwater levels, adversely affecting water availability and food security of the people.

Post-independent India witnessed intensive industrialisation and urbanisation, creating vast opportunities for us. Today, large industrial houses are as commonplace as the industrial units of many MNCs (Multinational Corporations). The ever-increasing number of industries has made matters worse by exerting pressure on existing freshwater resources. Industries, apart from being heavy users of water, also require power to run them; much of this energy comes from hydroelectric power. Moreover, multiplying urban centres with large and dense populations and urban lifestyles have not only added to water and energy requirements but have further aggravated the problem. Most housing societies or colonies in cities have their own groundwater pumping devices to meet their water needs, so fragile water resources are being over-exploited and have caused their depletion in several cities.

Qualitative scarcity — when there is water but it cannot be used

So far we have focused on the quantitative aspects of water scarcity. Now consider another situation where water is sufficiently available to meet the needs of the people, but the area still suffers from water scarcity. This scarcity may be due to bad quality of water. Lately, there has been a growing concern that even if there is ample water to meet the needs of the people, much of it may be polluted by domestic and industrial wastes, chemicals, pesticides and fertilisers used in agriculture, thus making it hazardous for human use.

Caption from the chapter

Water, Water Everywhere, Not a Drop to Drink: after a heavy downpour, a boy collects drinking water in Kolkata. Life in the city and its adjacent districts was paralysed as incessant overnight rain, meaning a record 180 mm, flooded a vast area and disrupted traffic.

The need of the hour is to conserve and manage our water resources, to safeguard ourselves from health hazards, to ensure food security, continuation of our livelihoods and productive activities, and also to prevent degradation of our natural ecosystems. Over-exploitation and mismanagement of water resources will impoverish this resource and cause an ecological crisis that may have a profound impact on our lives.

Government scheme

Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM): the Government of India has accorded the highest priority to improving the quality of life and enhancing the ease of living of people, especially those living in rural areas. The goal of JJM is to enable every rural household to get an assured supply of potable piped water at a service level of 55 litres per capita per day regularly on a long-term basis by ensuring functionality of the tap water connections. (Source: Economic Survey 2020–21, p. 357)

From your everyday experiences, write a short proposal on how you can conserve water.

Box: Hydraulic Structures in Ancient India

Archaeological and historical records show that from ancient times we have been constructing sophisticated hydraulic structures like dams built of stone rubble, reservoirs or lakes, embankments and canals for irrigation. Not surprisingly, we have continued this tradition in modern India by building dams in most of our river basins.

  • In the first century B.C., Sringaverapura near Allahabad had sophisticated water-harvesting system channelling the flood water of the river Ganga.
  • During the time of Chandragupta Maurya, dams, lakes and irrigation systems were extensively built.
  • Evidences of sophisticated irrigation works have also been found in Kalinga (Odisha), Nagarjunakonda (Andhra Pradesh), Bennur (Karnataka) and Kolhapur (Maharashtra).
  • In the 11th century, Bhopal Lake, one of the largest artificial lakes of its time, was built.
  • In the 13th–14th century, the tank in Hauz Khas, Delhi, was constructed by Allauddin Khilji for supplying water to the Siri Fort area.

Source: Dying Wisdom, CSE, 1997.

Sophisticated water-harvesting system channelling the flood water of the Ganga.
Dams, lakes and irrigation systems built extensively.

Multi-Purpose River Projects and Integrated Water Resources Management

How do we conserve and manage water? Dams were traditionally built to impound rivers and rainwater that could be used later to irrigate agricultural fields. Today, dams are built not just for irrigation but for electricity generation, water supply for domestic and industrial uses, flood control, recreation, inland navigation and fish breeding. Hence dams are now referred to as multi-purpose projects, where the many uses of the impounded water are integrated with one another.

For example, in the Sutlej–Beas river basin, the Bhakra–Nangal project water is being used both for hydel power production and irrigation. Similarly, the Hirakud project in the Mahanadi basin integrates conservation of water with flood control.

NCERT definition

Dam: a barrier across flowing water that obstructs, directs or retards the flow, often creating a reservoir, lake or impoundment. “Dam” refers to the reservoir rather than the structure. Most dams have a section called a spillway or weir over which or through which it is intended that water will flow either intermittently or continuously. Dams are classified according to structure, intended purpose or height. Based on structure and the materials used, dams are classified as timber dams, embankment dams or masonry dams, with several subtypes. According to height, dams can be categorised as large dams and major dams, or alternatively as low dams, medium height dams and high dams.

Multi-purpose projects, launched after Independence with their integrated water resources management approach, were thought of as the vehicle that would lead the nation to development and progress, overcoming the handicap of its colonial past. Jawaharlal Nehru proudly proclaimed the dams as the “temples of modern India”; the reason being that they would integrate the development of agriculture and the village economy with rapid industrialisation and the growth of the urban economy.

We have sown the crops in Asar
We will bring Bhadu in Bhadra
Floods have swollen the Damodar
The sailing boats cannot sail
Oh! Damodar, we fall at your feet
Reduce the floods a little
Bhadu will come a year later
Let the boats sail on your surface

— Popular Bhadu song of the Damodar valley region, narrating the troubles faced by people owing to the flooding of the Damodar river, known as the river of sorrow

Why Large Dams Are Criticised

In recent years, multi-purpose projects and large dams have come under great scrutiny and opposition for a variety of reasons.

  • Regulating and damming of rivers affects their natural flow, causing poor sediment flow and excessive sedimentation at the bottom of the reservoir, resulting in rockier stream beds and poorer habitats for the rivers’ aquatic life.
  • Dams also fragment rivers, making it difficult for aquatic fauna to migrate, especially for spawning.
  • The reservoirs created on the floodplains also submerge the existing vegetation and soil, leading to its decomposition over a period of time.
  • Ironically, the dams that were constructed to control floods have triggered floods due to sedimentation in the reservoir. Moreover, big dams have mostly been unsuccessful in controlling floods at the time of excessive rainfall.
  • These floods have not only devastated life and property but also caused extensive soil erosion.
  • Sedimentation also meant that the flood plains were deprived of silt, a natural fertiliser, further adding to the problem of land degradation.
  • It was also observed that multi-purpose projects induced earthquakes, caused water-borne diseases and pests and pollution resulting from excessive use of water.
  • Irrigation has changed the cropping pattern of many regions, with farmers shifting to water-intensive and commercial crops; this has great ecological consequences like salinisation of the soil.
Teacher explanation

Balanced view for exams: write the benefits (irrigation, hydel power, flood control, water supply, navigation, recreation, fish breeding) and then the costs (sedimentation, fragmentation, submergence, displacement, salinisation, induced earthquakes). A good answer always has both sides.

Government scheme

Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana ensures access to some means of protective irrigation for all agricultural farms in the country, thus bringing much-desired rural prosperity. Its broad objectives are to enhance the physical access of water on the farm and expand cultivable area under assured irrigation (har khet ko pani), improve on-farm water use efficiency to reduce wastage and increase availability both in duration and extent, promote irrigation and other water-saving technologies (per drop more crop) and introduce sustainable water conservation practices.

Box: Sardar Sarovar Dam and the Krishna–Godavari Dispute

Sardar Sarovar Dam has been built over the Narmada River in Gujarat. This is one of the largest water resource projects of India, covering four states — Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat and Rajasthan. The project would meet the requirement of water in drought-prone and desert areas.

Sardar Sarovar project — figures given in the chapter
ItemDetail
Irrigation in Gujarat18.45 lakh hectare of land, covering 3,112 villages in 15 districts
Irrigation in Rajasthan2,46,000 hectare in the desert districts of Barmer and Jalore
Irrigation in Maharashtra37,500 hectare in the tribal hilly tract, through lift
Drought-prone command areaAbout 75 per cent of the command area in Gujarat; the entire command in Rajasthan

Source: Sardar Sarovar Narmada Nigam Ltd., https://www.sardarsarovardam.org/

Krishna–Godavari dispute: the dispute is due to the objections raised by the Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh governments. It is regarding the diversion of more water at Koyna by the Maharashtra government for a multipurpose project. This would reduce downstream flow in their states, with adverse consequences for agriculture and industry.

Rainwater Harvesting

Many thought that given the disadvantages and rising resistance against multi-purpose projects, the water harvesting system was a viable alternative, both socio-economically and environmentally. In ancient India, along with the sophisticated hydraulic structures, there existed an extraordinary tradition of water-harvesting systems. People had in-depth knowledge of rainfall regimes and soil types and developed wide-ranging techniques to harvest rainwater, groundwater, river water and flood water in keeping with the local ecological conditions and their water needs.

Traditional rainwater harvesting methods named in the chapter
RegionMethodHow it works
Hill and mountainous regions (Western Himalayas)‘Guls’ or ‘kuls’Diversion channels built for agriculture; a kul leads to a circular village tank from which water is released as and when required.
Rajasthan (widely)Rooftop rainwater harvestingCommonly practised to store drinking water.
Flood plains of BengalInundation channelsDeveloped to irrigate fields.
Arid and semi-arid regionsRain-fed storage structuresAgricultural fields converted into structures that allow water to stand and moisten the soil — like the ‘khadins’ in Jaisalmer and ‘johads’ in other parts of Rajasthan.

The tankas of Rajasthan

In the semi-arid and arid regions of Rajasthan, particularly in Bikaner, Phalodi and Barmer, almost all the houses traditionally had underground tanks or tankas for storing drinking water. The tanks could be as large as a big room; one household in Phalodi had a tank that was 6.1 metres deep, 4.27 metres long and 2.44 metres wide. The tankas were part of the well-developed rooftop rainwater harvesting system and were built inside the main house or the courtyard. They were connected to the sloping roofs of the houses through a pipe. Rain falling on the rooftops would travel down the pipe and was stored in these underground tankas. The first spell of rain was usually not collected, as this would clean the roofs and the pipes; the rainwater from subsequent showers was then collected.

The rainwater can be stored in the tankas till the next rainfall, making it an extremely reliable source of drinking water when all other sources are dried up, particularly in summers. Rainwater, or palar pani, as it is commonly referred to in these parts, is considered the purest form of natural water. Many houses constructed underground rooms adjoining the tanka to beat the summer heat, as it would keep the room cool.

Today, in western Rajasthan, sadly the practice of rooftop rainwater harvesting is on the decline as plenty of water is available due to the perennial Indira Gandhi Canal, though some houses still maintain the tankas since they do not like the taste of tap water.

Rooftop harvesting elsewhere in India

In many parts of rural and urban India, rooftop rainwater harvesting is being successfully adapted to store and conserve water.

  • Tamil Nadu is the first state in India which has made rooftop rainwater harvesting structures compulsory for all houses across the state. There are legal provisions to punish defaulters.
  • Shillong, Meghalaya: rooftop rainwater harvesting is the most common practice. It is interesting because Cherapunjee and Mawsynram, situated at a distance of 55 km from Shillong, receive the highest rainfall in the world, yet the state capital faces acute shortage of water. Nearly every household has a rooftop harvesting structure, and nearly 15–25 per cent of the total water requirement of the household comes from rooftop water harvesting.
  • Gendathur, a remote backward village in Mysuru, Karnataka: villagers have installed rooftop rainwater harvesting systems to meet their water needs. Nearly 200 households have installed this system and the village has earned the rare distinction of being “rich in rainwater”. Gendathur receives an annual precipitation of 1,000 mm, and with 80 per cent collection efficiency and about 10 fillings, every house can collect and use about 50,000 litres of water annually. From the 200 houses, the net amount of rainwater harvested annually amounts to 1,00,000 litres (as stated in the chapter).
Activity

Find out other rainwater harvesting systems existing in and around your locality.

Teacher explanation

Read the Gendathur figures carefully. The chapter gives 50,000 litres per house and states the net amount for 200 houses as 1,00,000 litres. In an exam, quote the chapter’s figures as they are, and show your working separately if asked to calculate.

Box: Bamboo Drip Irrigation System

In Meghalaya, a 200-year-old system of tapping stream and spring water by using bamboo pipes is prevalent. About 18–20 litres of water enters the bamboo pipe system, gets transported over hundreds of metres, and finally reduces to 20–80 drops per minute at the site of the plant.

  • Picture 1: bamboo pipes are used to divert perennial springs on the hilltops to the lower reaches by gravity.
  • Pictures 2 and 3: channel sections made of bamboo divert water to the plant site where it is distributed into branches, again made and laid out with different forms of bamboo pipes. The flow of water into the pipes is controlled by manipulating the pipe positions.
  • Picture 4: if the pipes pass a road, they are taken high above the land.
  • Pictures 5 and 6: reduced channel sections and diversion units are used at the last stage of water application; the last channel section enables water to be dropped near the roots of the plant.

Key Terms and Definitions

Flashcards

All key terms

Key terms and definitions
TermSimple explanation
Hydrological cycleThe continuous movement of water within the earth and atmosphere, which renews and recharges surface run-off and groundwater, making water a renewable resource.
Surface run-offWater that flows over the land surface into streams, rivers and lakes instead of soaking into the ground.
GroundwaterWater stored below the ground in the pores and cracks of rock and soil, drawn up by wells and tube-wells.
Water scarcityShortage of usable water, caused in most cases by over-exploitation, excessive use and unequal access among social groups — or by bad quality of water.
Irrigated agricultureFarming with supplied water; the largest consumer of water.
Dry farmingFarming techniques suited to areas of low rainfall, using drought-resistant crops and moisture conservation instead of heavy irrigation.
Hydraulic structureA structure built to control, store or divert water — dams of stone rubble, reservoirs, lakes, embankments and canals.
DamA barrier across flowing water that obstructs, directs or retards the flow, often creating a reservoir, lake or impoundment; the word refers to the reservoir rather than the structure.
Spillway / weirThe section of a dam over or through which water is intended to flow intermittently or continuously.
Multi-purpose projectA project in which many uses of impounded water — irrigation, hydel power, water supply, flood control, recreation, inland navigation and fish breeding — are integrated.
SedimentationThe settling of silt and soil particles at the bottom of a reservoir, which reduces storage, creates rockier stream beds and can worsen floods.
SiltFine, fertile soil carried by rivers; when trapped in reservoirs, flood plains are deprived of this natural fertiliser.
SalinisationAccumulation of salts in the soil, often caused by over-irrigation and by a shift to water-intensive crops.
Jal Jeevan MissionA government mission to give every rural household an assured supply of potable piped water at 55 litres per capita per day.
Atal Bhujal Yojana (Atal Jal)A scheme in water-stressed Gram Panchayats to bring behavioural change from consumption to conservation and smart water management.
PMKSYPradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana — protective irrigation for all farms, “har khet ko pani” and “per drop more crop”.
Rainwater harvestingCollecting and storing rainwater for later use — on rooftops, in tanks, in fields or through channels.
Gul / kulDiversion channels built in hill and mountainous regions, especially the Western Himalayas, to carry stream water for agriculture.
KhadinA rain-fed storage structure in Jaisalmer where agricultural fields are converted so that water stands and moistens the soil.
JohadA similar rain-fed storage structure found in other parts of Rajasthan.
Inundation channelA channel developed in the flood plains of Bengal to irrigate fields with flood water.
TankaAn underground tank in Rajasthan, built inside the house or courtyard and connected to the sloping roof by a pipe, for storing drinking water.
Palar paniThe local name in western Rajasthan for rainwater, considered the purest form of natural water.
Bamboo drip irrigationA 200-year-old system in Meghalaya that taps stream and spring water through bamboo pipes, delivering 20–80 drops per minute at the plant.

NCERT In-text Questions and Answers

The questions printed inside the chapter

These are the “Can you…” and activity questions that appear inside the chapter text. Model answers are based on the chapter itself.

1.

If three-fourths of the world is covered with water and water is a renewable resource, how is it that countries and regions around the globe suffer from water scarcity?

Model answer

Because renewable does not mean unlimited at every place and time. Freshwater is a small share of total water, and its availability varies over space and time with seasonal and annual precipitation. In most cases scarcity is caused by over-exploitation, excessive use and unequal access among social groups, and by pollution that makes available water unusable.

2.

Is it possible that an area or region may have ample water resources but is still facing water scarcity? Give examples.

Model answer

Yes. Many of our cities have ample water resources but still face scarcity, because of large and growing populations, over-exploitation of groundwater by housing societies and industries, and unequal access. Water may also be too polluted to use — the chapter calls this scarcity due to bad quality of water.

3.

What are dams and how do they help us in conserving and managing water?

Model answer

A dam is a barrier across flowing water that obstructs, directs or retards the flow, often creating a reservoir, lake or impoundment. Traditionally dams impounded river and rainwater for irrigation; today they also generate electricity, supply water for domestic and industrial use, control floods, provide recreation, inland navigation and fish breeding. Such integrated projects are called multi-purpose projects.

4.

From your everyday experiences, write a short proposal on how you can conserve water.

Model answer

Model proposal: (i) fix leaking taps and use buckets instead of running hoses; (ii) take shorter showers and turn off taps while brushing; (iii) reuse water from washing vegetables for plants; (iv) install a rooftop rainwater harvesting structure or a simple drum at the drainpipe; (v) harvest rainwater in the school ground by making a recharge pit; (vi) report leaking public taps; (vii) water plants in the evening to reduce evaporation. (Student answers will vary.)

5.

Find out more about any one traditional method of building dams and irrigation works.

Model answer

Example — the khadin of Jaisalmer: a long earthen embankment is built across a slope so that rainwater from the catchment collects and stands on the agricultural field behind it; the moisture soaks into the soil and a crop is grown on residual moisture. Similar structures are called johads in other parts of Rajasthan. (Student answers may describe kuls, tankas or inundation channels.)

6.

Find out other rainwater harvesting systems existing in and around your locality.

Model answer

Common examples: rooftop harvesting with a storage tank or recharge pit; percolation tanks and recharge wells in colonies; check dams and farm ponds in villages; storage of rainwater in temple tanks; and, in hilly areas, diversion channels like guls. (Student answers will vary.)

7.

Collect information about floods that occurred in different parts of the country due to heavy rainfall in recent times.

Model answer

The chapter itself records the Assam floods and the record 180 mm overnight rain that flooded Kolkata, and the newspaper page reproduced in the chapter reports floods in Maharashtra, Jammu and Kolkata. Collect recent newspaper reports, note the date, place, rainfall, damage and relief measures. (Student answers will vary.)

8.

Make a list of inter-state water disputes.

Model answer

The chapter names the Krishna–Godavari dispute (Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh objecting to Maharashtra diverting more water at Koyna). Other well-known disputes in the news include the Cauvery dispute between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu and the Ravi–Beas dispute between Punjab and Haryana. (The chapter discusses only the Krishna–Godavari dispute in detail.)

9.

Collect information on how industries are polluting our water resources, and enact a scene of a water dispute in your locality.

Model answer

Industries discharge organic and inorganic wastes, dyes, detergents, acids, salts and heavy metals into rivers, and hot water from factories causes thermal pollution. Students can dramatise a dispute between farmers, a factory and a municipal body over the use of a local stream. (Student activity.)

NCERT Exercises

Reproduced from the exercise section of the chapter, with model answers. Word limits are the ones the textbook sets.

1.
NCERT exercise2 marks

Multiple choice — Based on the information given below, classify each situation as “suffering from water scarcity” or “not suffering from water scarcity”. (a) Region with high annual rainfall. (b) Region having high annual rainfall and large population. (c) Region having high annual rainfall but water is highly polluted. (d) Region having low rainfall and low population.

Model answer

(a) Not suffering — plenty of rainfall with no stated pressure on it. (b) Suffering — a large population raises demand beyond supply and causes over-exploitation. (c) Suffering — qualitative scarcity: water is available but unusable because it is highly polluted. (d) Generally not suffering — low rainfall, but demand is also low; scarcity would arise only if use exceeded availability.

2.
NCERT exercise1 mark

Multiple choice — Which one of the following statements is not an argument in favour of multi-purpose river projects? (a) They bring water to areas which suffer from water scarcity. (b) By regulating water flow they help to control floods. (c) They lead to large-scale displacements and loss of livelihood. (d) They generate electricity for our industries and homes.

Model answer

(c) They lead to large-scale displacements and loss of livelihood. This is a criticism of multi-purpose projects, not an argument in their favour.

3.
NCERT exercise3 marks

Here are some false statements. Identify the mistakes and rewrite them correctly. (a) Multiplying urban centres with large and dense populations and urban lifestyles have helped in proper utilisation of water resources. (b) Regulating and damming of rivers does not affect the river’s natural flow and its sediment flow. (c) Today in Rajasthan, the practice of rooftop rainwater harvesting has gained popularity despite high water availability due to the Indira Gandhi Canal.

Model answer

(a) Multiplying urban centres with large and dense populations and urban lifestyles have added to water and energy requirements and further aggravated the problem of water scarcity. (b) Regulating and damming of rivers does affect the river’s natural flow and its sediment flow, causing poor sediment flow and excessive sedimentation in the reservoir. (c) Today in Rajasthan, the practice of rooftop rainwater harvesting has declined because plenty of water is available due to the perennial Indira Gandhi Canal, though some houses still maintain tankas.

4.
NCERT exercise2 marks

Explain how water becomes a renewable resource. (about 30 words)

Model answer

Freshwater is continually renewed and recharged through the hydrological cycle: water evaporates, forms clouds, falls as rain and returns to surface run-off and groundwater. Since all water moves within this cycle, water is a renewable resource.

5.
NCERT exercise2 marks

What is water scarcity and what are its main causes? (about 30 words)

Model answer

Water scarcity is the shortage of usable water. Its main causes are over-exploitation, excessive use and unequal access among social groups, large and growing populations, and pollution that makes available water hazardous for use.

6.
NCERT exercise3 marks

Compare the advantages and disadvantages of multi-purpose river projects. (about 30 words)

Model answer

Advantages: irrigation, hydel power, domestic and industrial water supply, flood control, recreation, inland navigation and fish breeding. Disadvantages: sedimentation, fragmented rivers and poor aquatic habitats, submergence of vegetation and soil, induced floods, salinisation, earthquakes, water-borne diseases and displacement.

7.
NCERT exercise5 marks

Discuss how rainwater harvesting in semi-arid regions of Rajasthan is carried out. (about 120 words)

Model answer

In the semi-arid and arid regions of Rajasthan, particularly Bikaner, Phalodi and Barmer, almost all houses traditionally had underground tankas for storing drinking water. The tankas were part of a well-developed rooftop rainwater harvesting system, built inside the main house or in the courtyard and connected to the sloping roofs through a pipe. Rain falling on the roof travelled down the pipe and was stored in the tanka; the first spell of rain was not collected, as it cleaned the roofs and pipes. A tanka could be as large as a big room — one in Phalodi was 6.1 m deep, 4.27 m long and 2.44 m wide. The water lasted till the next rainfall and was a reliable source in summer. This rainwater, called palar pani, is considered the purest natural water, and adjoining underground rooms stayed cool. The practice is now declining because of the perennial Indira Gandhi Canal.

8.
NCERT exercise5 marks

Describe how modern adaptations of traditional rainwater harvesting methods are being carried out to conserve and store water. (about 120 words)

Model answer

Traditional methods are being revived and adapted. Rooftop rainwater harvesting is now common in rural and urban India: rainwater is collected from roofs through PVC pipes, filtered through sand and bricks, taken to a sump for immediate use, and the excess is directed to a well to recharge groundwater — as shown for recharge through a hand pump or an abandoned dugwell. Tamil Nadu is the first state to make rooftop harvesting compulsory for all houses, with legal provisions to punish defaulters. In Shillong, nearly every household has such a structure and 15–25 per cent of household water comes from it. In Gendathur (Mysuru, Karnataka) about 200 households have installed the system, and with 1,000 mm rainfall and 80 per cent efficiency each house can collect about 50,000 litres a year. Bamboo drip irrigation in Meghalaya continues a 200-year-old tradition.

09

Important Questions and Answers

Board-style practice

Practice questions

Written in the style of CBSE board papers. They are additional practice, not NCERT originals.

1.

Explain any three causes of water scarcity. (3 marks)

Model answer

(i) Over-exploitation and excessive use — tube-wells, industries and housing societies pump groundwater faster than it recharges, lowering water tables. (ii) Large and growing population — more water is needed for domestic use and to grow more food, so irrigated areas expand. (iii) Unequal access to water among different social groups, and pollution of available water by domestic and industrial wastes, chemicals, pesticides and fertilisers, which makes it hazardous to use.

2.

Why is irrigated agriculture called the largest consumer of water? What should be done? (3 marks)

Model answer

To facilitate higher food-grain production, water resources are over-exploited to expand irrigated areas for dry-season agriculture, and farmers sink wells and tube-wells, which lowers groundwater levels. The chapter suggests revolutionising agriculture through drought-resistant crops and dry farming techniques, and improving on-farm water-use efficiency — “per drop more crop” under PMKSY.

3.

Describe the hydraulic structures of ancient India. (5 marks)

Model answer

In the first century B.C., Sringaverapura near Allahabad had a sophisticated water-harvesting system channelling the flood water of the Ganga. During the time of Chandragupta Maurya, dams, lakes and irrigation systems were extensively built. Evidence of sophisticated irrigation works has been found in Kalinga (Odisha), Nagarjunakonda (Andhra Pradesh), Bennur (Karnataka) and Kolhapur (Maharashtra). In the 11th century, Bhopal Lake, one of the largest artificial lakes of its time, was built. In the 13th–14th century, the tank in Hauz Khas, Delhi, was constructed by Allauddin Khilji for supplying water to the Siri Fort area.

4.

Define a dam. How are dams classified? (3 marks)

Model answer

A dam is a barrier across flowing water that obstructs, directs or retards the flow, often creating a reservoir, lake or impoundment; the word refers to the reservoir rather than the structure. Most dams have a spillway or weir through which water flows intermittently or continuously. Dams are classified according to structure, intended purpose or height. By structure and materials they are timber, embankment or masonry dams; by height they are large and major dams, or low, medium-height and high dams.

5.

Why did Jawaharlal Nehru call dams the “temples of modern India”? (2 marks)

Model answer

Because multi-purpose projects were expected to integrate the development of agriculture and the village economy with rapid industrialisation and the growth of the urban economy, and thus lead the nation to development and progress, overcoming the handicap of its colonial past.

6.

Explain any four problems created by large dams. (4 marks)

Model answer

(i) They affect the natural flow of rivers, causing poor sediment flow and excessive sedimentation in reservoirs, rockier stream beds and poorer habitats for aquatic life. (ii) They fragment rivers, making it difficult for aquatic fauna to migrate, especially for spawning. (iii) Reservoirs submerge existing vegetation and soil, which decomposes over time. (iv) Dams built to control floods have themselves triggered floods because of sedimentation, and have been unsuccessful in controlling floods in excessive rainfall. Also: flood plains are deprived of silt, multi-purpose projects induced earthquakes, water-borne diseases and pests, and irrigation has led to a shift to water-intensive crops and salinisation of soil.

7.

What is rainwater harvesting? Describe any three traditional methods. (5 marks)

Model answer

Rainwater harvesting is the collection and storage of rainwater for later use. Traditional methods: (i) in hill and mountainous regions people built diversion channels like the guls or kuls of the Western Himalayas for agriculture; (ii) rooftop rainwater harvesting was commonly practised to store drinking water, particularly in Rajasthan, where underground tankas were built inside the house or courtyard and connected to sloping roofs; (iii) in the flood plains of Bengal, inundation channels were developed to irrigate fields; and (iv) in arid and semi-arid regions, fields were converted into rain-fed storage structures such as the khadins of Jaisalmer and johads of other parts of Rajasthan.

8.

Describe rooftop rainwater harvesting in Shillong and Gendathur. (5 marks)

Model answer

Shillong: rooftop rainwater harvesting is the most common practice. It is interesting because Cherapunjee and Mawsynram, only 55 km away, receive the highest rainfall in the world, yet Shillong faces acute water shortage. Nearly every household has a rooftop structure and nearly 15–25 per cent of total household water requirement comes from it. Gendathur (Mysuru, Karnataka): a remote backward village where nearly 200 households installed rooftop rainwater harvesting systems and earned the distinction of being “rich in rainwater”. With 1,000 mm annual precipitation, 80 per cent collection efficiency and about 10 fillings, each house can collect about 50,000 litres a year; the chapter states the net amount harvested by the 200 houses as 1,00,000 litres annually.

9.

Why did Tamil Nadu make rooftop rainwater harvesting compulsory? (2 marks)

Model answer

To conserve and store water: Tamil Nadu is the first state to make rooftop rainwater harvesting structures compulsory for all houses across the state, with legal provisions to punish defaulters.

10.

Describe the bamboo drip irrigation system of Meghalaya. (3 marks)

Model answer

It is a 200-year-old system of tapping stream and spring water using bamboo pipes. About 18–20 litres of water enters the bamboo pipe system, is transported over hundreds of metres, and reduces to 20–80 drops per minute at the plant. Bamboo channel sections divert water to the plant site and distribute it through branches; flow is controlled by manipulating pipe positions; where pipes cross a road they are taken high above the land; and reduced channel sections and diversion units drop water near the roots.

11.

What is the Sardar Sarovar project and which states does it cover? (3 marks)

Model answer

Sardar Sarovar Dam is built over the Narmada River in Gujarat and is one of the largest water resource projects of India, covering Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat and Rajasthan. It will provide irrigation to 18.45 lakh hectares covering 3,112 villages in 15 districts of Gujarat, 2,46,000 hectares in Barmer and Jalore (Rajasthan) and 37,500 hectares in the tribal hilly tract of Maharashtra through lift. About 75 per cent of the command area in Gujarat and the entire command in Rajasthan is drought prone.

12.

Explain the Krishna–Godavari water dispute. (2 marks)

Model answer

The dispute is due to objections raised by the Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh governments to the diversion of more water at Koyna by the Maharashtra government for a multipurpose project. This would reduce downstream flow in their states, with adverse consequences for agriculture and industry.

10

Previous Year Questions (PYQs)

Asked in CBSE board exams

Previous year questions

These follow the pattern of questions set in CBSE Social Science papers for this chapter. Answers are model answers.

1.
CBSE pattern

“Water is a renewable resource, yet we face water scarcity.” Explain. (CBSE pattern, 3 marks)

Model answer

Water is renewable because it is continually renewed and recharged through the hydrological cycle. But freshwater is only a small part of total water, and its availability varies over space and time with precipitation. Scarcity in most cases is caused by over-exploitation, excessive use and unequal access among social groups, by large and growing populations demanding more water for domestic use and food production, and by pollution that makes available water hazardous.

2.
CBSE pattern

Mention any three traditional water-harvesting structures of India with their regions. (3 marks)

Model answer

(i) Guls or kuls — diversion channels of the Western Himalayas. (ii) Khadins (Jaisalmer) and johads (other parts of Rajasthan) — rain-fed storage structures in arid and semi-arid regions. (iii) Tankas — underground tanks for rooftop rainwater in Bikaner, Phalodi and Barmer; also inundation channels in the flood plains of Bengal.

3.
CBSE pattern

Why have multi-purpose projects come under scrutiny? Give any three reasons. (3 marks)

Model answer

(i) They affect the natural flow of rivers and cause excessive sedimentation, poorer aquatic habitats and fragmented rivers that block fish migration. (ii) Reservoirs submerge vegetation and soil, and dams built for flood control have themselves triggered floods. (iii) They have displaced people and affected livelihoods, induced earthquakes and water-borne diseases, and irrigation has led to salinisation of soil.

4.
CBSE pattern

Explain the objectives of the Jal Jeevan Mission. (2 marks)

Model answer

To enable every rural household to get an assured supply of potable piped water at a service level of 55 litres per capita per day, regularly on a long-term basis, by ensuring the functionality of tap water connections.

5.
CBSE pattern

What is Atal Bhujal Yojana? Where is it being implemented? (3 marks)

Model answer

Atal Bhujal Yojana (Atal Jal) is being implemented in 8,220 water-stressed Gram Panchayats of 229 administrative blocks/talukas in 80 districts of seven states — Gujarat, Haryana, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh. These states account for about 37 per cent of India’s water-stressed blocks. A key aspect is to bring behavioural change in the community from consumption to conservation and smart water management.

6.
CBSE pattern

What are the objectives of the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana? (3 marks)

Model answer

To ensure access to protective irrigation for all agricultural farms; enhance physical access of water on the farm and expand cultivable area under assured irrigation (“har khet ko pani”); improve on-farm water-use efficiency to reduce wastage and increase availability in duration and extent; promote water-saving technologies (“per drop more crop”); and introduce sustainable water conservation practices.

7.
CBSE pattern

How has irrigation changed cropping patterns and with what consequences? (2 marks)

Model answer

Farmers have shifted to water-intensive and commercial crops, which has great ecological consequences such as salinisation of the soil.

8.
CBSE pattern

Describe the tanka system of Rajasthan. (3 marks)

Model answer

Tankas are underground tanks for storing drinking water, built inside the main house or courtyard and connected to sloping roofs by a pipe. Rain from the roof flows down the pipe into the tanka; the first spell is not collected as it cleans the roof and pipe. Water is stored till the next rainfall and is called palar pani, considered the purest natural water. One tanka in Phalodi was 6.1 m deep, 4.27 m long and 2.44 m wide.

9.
CBSE pattern

Why is rooftop rainwater harvesting declining in western Rajasthan? (1 mark)

Model answer

Because plenty of water is available from the perennial Indira Gandhi Canal, though some houses still maintain tankas as they do not like the taste of tap water.

10.
CBSE pattern

Give an example of an inter-state water dispute and explain its cause. (2 marks)

Model answer

The Krishna–Godavari dispute: Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh object to Maharashtra diverting more water at Koyna for a multipurpose project, which would reduce downstream flow in their states and harm agriculture and industry.

11

Frequently Asked Questions

Quick clarifications

1.

Is water scarcity only about low rainfall?

Model answer

No. Low and variable rainfall matters, but in most cases scarcity is caused by over-exploitation, excessive use and unequal access to water among different social groups, and by pollution of available water.

2.

What exactly is a multi-purpose project?

Model answer

A project in which many uses of the impounded water — irrigation, hydel power, domestic and industrial supply, flood control, recreation, inland navigation and fish breeding — are integrated with one another.

3.

Are dams good or bad according to the chapter?

Model answer

Both. They provide irrigation, power and flood control and were called “temples of modern India”, but they also cause sedimentation, fragment rivers, submerge land, displace people, trigger floods and salinise soils. A good answer gives both sides.

4.

Why is the first spell of rain not collected?

Model answer

Because it cleans the roofs and pipes, so the water from it is discarded; rainwater from subsequent showers is collected in the tanka.

5.

Why does Shillong face water shortage when Cherapunjee is so near?

Model answer

The chapter notes the paradox — Cherapunjee and Mawsynram, 55 km away, receive the highest rainfall in the world, yet Shillong faces acute shortage. Its response is rooftop rainwater harvesting: nearly every household has such a structure and 15–25 per cent of household water comes from it.

6.

Which state made rooftop rainwater harvesting compulsory?

Model answer

Tamil Nadu — the first state in India, with legal provisions to punish defaulters.

7.

What is palar pani?

Model answer

The local name in western Rajasthan for rainwater, considered the purest form of natural water.

8.

What is the difference between a khadin and a johad?

Model answer

Both are rain-fed storage structures of Rajasthan in which fields are converted so that water stands and moistens the soil. Khadins are specifically those of Jaisalmer; johads are found in other parts of Rajasthan.

Assertion-Reason Questions

Choose the correct option

How to answer

(a) Both A and R are true and R explains A. (b) Both are true but R does not explain A. (c) A is true, R is false. (d) A is false, R is true.

1.

Assertion (A): Water is a renewable resource.
Reason (R): Water is continually renewed and recharged through the hydrological cycle.

2.

Assertion (A): Water scarcity occurs even in regions with ample water resources.
Reason (R): Water scarcity in most cases is caused by over-exploitation, excessive use and unequal access.

3.

Assertion (A): Irrigated agriculture is the largest consumer of water.
Reason (R): Water resources are over-exploited to expand irrigated areas for dry-season agriculture.

4.

Assertion (A): Dams are called the “temples of modern India”.
Reason (R): Jawaharlal Nehru said this because dams would integrate agricultural development with industrialisation.

5.

Assertion (A): Large dams have successfully controlled floods in all cases.
Reason (R): Sedimentation in reservoirs has triggered floods.

6.

Assertion (A): Dams affect aquatic life.
Reason (R): Dams fragment rivers, making it difficult for aquatic fauna to migrate, especially for spawning.

7.

Assertion (A): Rooftop rainwater harvesting is gaining popularity in western Rajasthan.
Reason (R): The perennial Indira Gandhi Canal supplies plenty of water there.

8.

Assertion (A): Tamil Nadu has made rooftop rainwater harvesting compulsory.
Reason (R): Tamil Nadu is the first state to do so, with legal provisions to punish defaulters.

9.

Assertion (A): The bamboo drip irrigation system of Meghalaya is very old.
Reason (R): It is a 200-year-old system of tapping stream and spring water using bamboo pipes.

10.

Assertion (A): Water scarcity can be caused by bad quality of water.
Reason (R): Water may be polluted by domestic and industrial wastes, chemicals, pesticides and fertilisers, making it hazardous for human use.

Source-Based and Case-Based Questions

Read the passage or table, then answer

Source 1 — The Bhadu song of the Damodar valley

Source extract
We have sown the crops in Asar / We will bring Bhadu in Bhadra / Floods have swollen the Damodar / The sailing boats cannot sail / Oh! Damodar, we fall at your feet / Reduce the floods a little / Bhadu will come a year later / Let the boats sail on your surface

This popular Bhadu song in the Damodar valley region narrates the troubles faced by people owing to the flooding of the Damodar river, known as the river of sorrow.

1.

Which river is the song about and what is it called?

Model answer

The Damodar, known as the “river of sorrow”.

2.

What troubles do the people describe?

Model answer

Floods that swell the river so that sailing boats cannot sail; the people appeal to the river to reduce the floods a little.

3.

How does this song support the case for dams, and how does it warn against them?

Model answer

It supports dams because flood control is one of the stated purposes of multi-purpose projects such as Hirakud on the Mahanadi. It warns, though, that regulating a river changes the lives of people who depend on it, and the chapter notes that dams built for flood control have themselves triggered floods through sedimentation.

Source 2 — Newspaper page on floods

Case study (page 7)

The chapter reproduces a newspaper page headed “FLOODS — Basic Safety Precautions To Be Taken”. It advises: listen to radio/TV for weather bulletins and pass on the information; keep a family emergency kit with portable radio, torch, spare batteries, first-aid box, ORS, dry food, drinking water, matches and candles; keep ropes, rubber tubes, umbrella and bamboo stick; keep valuables and documents safe; move to relief camps or elevated places; turn off power and gas before leaving. During floods: do not enter flood waters; keep children away; stay away from sewerage lines, gutters and drains; be careful of snakes; stay away from electric poles and fallen power lines; do not use wet electrical appliances; eat freshly cooked dry food; use boiled and filtered water; keep drains clean; stagnation breeds vector and water-borne diseases; use bleaching powder and lime to disinfect.

1.

Why does the chapter place a flood-safety page in a chapter on water resources?

Model answer

Because water is both a resource and a hazard: the chapter shows floods devastating life and property, and the same water must be managed — stored, diverted and harvested — to reduce damage.

2.

Name three precautions to be taken before a flood.

Model answer

Any three: listen to weather bulletins and warn others; prepare a family emergency kit; keep valuables and documents safe; move to relief camps or elevated ground; switch off power and gas before leaving.

3.

Why is drinking water a special concern during floods?

Model answer

Because flood water contaminates sources, and stagnation breeds vector and water-borne diseases; the advice is to use boiled and filtered water and to disinfect with bleaching powder and lime.

Source 3 — Data: Gendathur’s rooftop harvest

1.

What does “80 per cent collection efficiency” mean here?

Model answer

That four-fifths of the rain falling on the roof area is actually collected; a fifth is lost through spillage, evaporation and the discarded first spell.

2.

Why is Gendathur described as “rich in rainwater”?

Model answer

Because about 200 households harvest rainwater on their rooftops, making the village self-reliant in water even though it is a remote, backward village.

3.

Which two conditions make rooftop harvesting worthwhile in a place like Gendathur?

Model answer

Adequate annual rainfall (1,000 mm) and a storage or recharge arrangement that can hold the collected water (about 10 fillings a year).

HOTS and Competency-Based Questions

Think beyond the text

Higher order thinking

These ask you to apply, compare or evaluate. Model answers are indicative — your own well-reasoned answer can differ.

1.

A city has a full reservoir but its residents still queue for water. Using this chapter, explain at least three possible reasons.

Model answer

(i) Unequal access — some localities and housing societies have their own pumping devices while others do not. (ii) Bad quality — the stored water may be polluted by domestic and industrial waste and unsafe to drink. (iii) Losses and mismanagement — leakages in distribution, and over-exploitation of groundwater elsewhere. (iv) Demand pressure from a large population and water-intensive agriculture or industry nearby. (Model answer.)

2.

“Every large dam is a bargain with nature.” Explain this statement with reference to the chapter.

Model answer

A dam gives irrigation, hydel power, water supply, flood control, navigation and fish breeding — that is the bargain. In return, nature and people pay: the river’s natural flow and sediment flow change, reservoirs silt up, rivers are fragmented and fish cannot migrate, vegetation and soil are submerged, flood plains lose fertile silt, salinity rises with irrigation, and some projects have induced earthquakes and disease. The bargain is worth making only if these costs are planned for. (Model answer.)

3.

Compare the tanka of Rajasthan with rooftop harvesting in a modern city apartment. What problems does the city face that the tanka did not?

Model answer

Both collect rain from the roof through a pipe and store it. The tanka stored water underground inside the house, kept it cool and lasted till the next monsoon — a single-family, low-density solution. A city apartment has a shared roof, limited space, and a large number of households; storage must be centralised, and much of the roof area is not connected to a tank. Cities therefore usually recharge groundwater through pits and wells rather than store water, and need rules (as in Tamil Nadu) plus maintenance to prevent contamination. (Model answer.)

4.

The chapter says irrigated agriculture is the largest consumer of water, yet India needs more food. Suggest a way out.

Model answer

Improve efficiency rather than expand area: drought-resistant crops and dry farming techniques; “per drop more crop” through drip and sprinkler irrigation under PMKSY; repairing canal systems to reduce seepage; growing crops suited to local rainfall; and rainwater harvesting and groundwater recharge so that the same water serves more than one use. Also avoid water-intensive crops in dry regions, which is what causes salinisation. (Model answer.)

5.

Why is a 200-year-old bamboo pipe system in Meghalaya still relevant today?

Model answer

Because it delivers water precisely to the plant with almost no energy cost — the flow is by gravity, and 18–20 litres entering the system reduce to 20–80 drops per minute at the root. It uses local material, needs no electricity, and avoids evaporation and runoff losses. It is an example of the chapter’s argument that traditional knowledge of rainfall and soils is often more appropriate than large structures. (Model answer.)

6.

If you were asked to prepare a water plan for a drought-prone district, what would you include? Use at least four ideas from the chapter.

Model answer

(i) Rainwater harvesting — rooftop systems, khadins or farm ponds, and recharge pits or wells. (ii) Revival of traditional structures such as tankas and johads, with maintenance. (iii) Efficient irrigation — drip and sprinkler, drought-resistant crops, dry farming. (iv) Regulation of groundwater extraction by industry and housing societies, with community monitoring. (v) A watershed or check-dam approach to hold run-off. (vi) Awareness and behavioural change from consumption to conservation, as Atal Bhujal Yojana attempts. (Model answer.)

18

Quick Revision Sheet

One page before the exam

Water as a resource

  • Three-fourths of earth is water; only a small share is usable freshwater.
  • Surface run-off and groundwater, renewed through the hydrological cycle → renewable.
  • Prediction: nearly two billion people in absolute water scarcity by 2025.

Scarcity

  • Quantitative: over-exploitation, excessive use, unequal access, growing population.
  • Irrigated agriculture is the largest consumer; groundwater falling; industries and cities add pressure.
  • Qualitative: pollution by domestic and industrial waste, chemicals, pesticides, fertilisers.

Ancient hydraulic structures

  • 1st century B.C. Sringaverapura (Allahabad); Chandragupta Maurya; Kalinga, Nagarjunakonda, Bennur, Kolhapur.
  • 11th century Bhopal Lake; 13th–14th century Hauz Khas by Allauddin Khilji.

Dams and multi-purpose projects

  • Dam = barrier; spillway/weir; classified by structure, purpose, height.
  • Uses: irrigation, hydel power, water supply, flood control, recreation, inland navigation, fish breeding.
  • Bhakra–Nangal (Sutlej–Beas), Hirakud (Mahanadi). Nehru: “temples of modern India”.

Criticism of dams

  • Sedimentation, rockier beds, fragmented rivers, submergence, induced floods, silt loss, salinisation, earthquakes, disease, displacement.

Schemes

  • Jal Jeevan Mission — 55 litres per capita per day to rural households.
  • Atal Bhujal Yojana — 8,220 Gram Panchayats, 7 states, behavioural change.
  • PMKSY — har khet ko pani, per drop more crop.

Rainwater harvesting

  • Guls/kuls (Western Himalayas); rooftop (Rajasthan); inundation channels (Bengal); khadins (Jaisalmer), johads (Rajasthan).
  • Tankas: Bikaner, Phalodi, Barmer; palar pani; first spell not collected.
  • Tamil Nadu compulsory; Shillong 15–25%; Gendathur 200 houses, 1,000 mm, 80%, 50,000 litres/house.
  • Decline in western Rajasthan due to Indira Gandhi Canal.
  • Bamboo drip irrigation, Meghalaya — 200 years, 18–20 litres to 20–80 drops/min.

Chapter Summary

The whole chapter in a few paragraphs

Three-fourths of the earth’s surface is water, but only a small part is usable freshwater, obtained from surface run-off and groundwater renewed through the hydrological cycle. Water is therefore renewable — yet scarcity is widespread, and by 2025 nearly two billion people are predicted to live in absolute water scarcity. In most cases scarcity is caused by over-exploitation, excessive use and unequal access among social groups; growing populations, expanding irrigated agriculture (the largest consumer of water), industries and cities add pressure; and pollution creates a scarcity of usable water even where water is abundant.

India has a long tradition of hydraulic structures — from Sringaverapura in the first century B.C. and the works of Chandragupta Maurya’s time, through Bhopal Lake in the eleventh century, to the Hauz Khas tank of Allauddin Khilji. Modern India built dams: Bhakra–Nangal on the Sutlej–Beas for hydel power and irrigation, Hirakud on the Mahanadi for water conservation with flood control, and many others, which Nehru called the “temples of modern India”. But large dams are now criticised for sedimentation, fragmenting rivers, submerging land, triggering floods, depriving flood plains of silt, salinisation, induced earthquakes and disease, and displacement. Government schemes such as the Jal Jeevan Mission, Atal Bhujal Yojana and PMKSY now stress assured supply, groundwater conservation and efficient use.

Rainwater harvesting is the other great tradition: guls and kuls in the hills, inundation channels in Bengal, khadins and johads in Rajasthan, and the underground tankas connected to sloping roofs, where the first spell of rain is discarded and palar pani is stored for summer. Today Tamil Nadu makes rooftop harvesting compulsory, Shillong harvests 15–25 per cent of its household water from roofs, and Gendathur in Karnataka is “rich in rainwater”. Meghalaya’s 200-year-old bamboo drip irrigation, delivering 20–80 drops a minute at the plant, shows how appropriate technology can conserve water with almost no energy cost.
